_source: Fortune & Fall 'Why Everyone Bought a Stanley, and Why They Stopped', 84K views in 10 days. Watched in the built-in browser 2026-11-19: frames 0-67 s every 3-7 s plus a 0.5 s burst at 22-23.5 s, then 150/300/420/530/615/800/870 s; word timings from YouTube's transcript panel (2,464 words over 869 s, about 170 a minute). No sound probe on this one (same channel as V6-3wqQoxT0, measured there). Our own descriptions; shots after 67 s are spot samples.

hook.firstFrame: black, fading up on phone footage of a hand dropping a big tumbler into a car cup holder
hook.firstLine: You have seen this cup everywhere; it may be in your kitchen now.

lines.gist: Points at a cup the viewer knows and probably owns.
A shelved product; three bloggers buy thousands and sell out in days.
Sales go up tenfold; store stampedes and resale markups.
Then demand cools and the boss calls it a settling.
It wasn't luck on social media; two machines did it, and you'll see them.
A century-old flask brand, the neglected cup and the bloggers who noticed it.
Affiliate links and limited colour drops turn a cup into a collectible.
A psychology study on scarcity, then a viral car-fire video and a stunt reply.
Stampedes, a lead scare, lawsuits, and the architect leaves.
Online sales halve and the whole category stops growing.
Why the scarcity flipped, and the brand's next bets.
Returns to the three bloggers and asks what is rationed next.

ending.lastFrame: the opening's car cup-holder footage returns with a phone card

whyItWorks: First line points at an object in the viewer's hand, then gives the before-and-after in under a minute.
One branded backdrop (blueprint grid) holds product cut-outs, phone cards and charts, so the whole video reads as one set.
Chart changes keep the ghost of the old value (dashed outline), so a drop reads at a glance.
Every claim carries a source chip or a highlighted article screenshot, which makes it feel investigated.
